headline: The architecture move is **not** the next stage — but one third of it is, and that third is not React. Decomposed, the owner's three drivers separate cleanly: **navigation** needs a serializable panel-descriptor registry (already fully specified in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-24-navigation-model-design.md`) which React does *not* give you — React Router would demand the exact same 57-surface conversion, done blind, with the 271 CSS locators broken at the same time; **multi-device sync** needs Worker hardening + a versioned keyspace + accounts, to which React contributes literally zero; **React itself** buys only a better render layer, and the render layer is the *one* part of this codebase that is genuinely disposable (~1,085 HTML-bearing lines, 104 `innerHTML` sites out of 11,564). So the honest answer to "אם התוצאה תהיה כתיבה מחדש חבל על העבודה" is: **nothing has to be thrown away except the HTML-string rendering — provided we extract NAV, ORCH and RULES as framework-agnostic modules *first*, which is work we already committed to for other reasons.** React is a scheduled *last* step, not the next one, and it is only worth doing if the owner wants it for reasons beyond the three he named.
recommendation:
**Twelve phases, each ending in a shipped vNNN. Order is fixed by dependency and rework, not preference.**

**P0 · Wave 0 (6 units).** The three approved bugs. Wrap-trigger becomes a real stage (`advanceWhen:{coreC}`) — this is a *safety-adjacent equipment bug shipped in production today* (`deriveRequires` emits no butcher-paper/foil requirement, so E3 calls a brisket cook "valid" for a user who owns neither), and it is a hard prerequisite for the owner's CP2 clarification ("the device sequence in the correct order in the work plan" is missing its central step without it). Plus `svOrderDesc` wiring and the `validCombo` fall-through. Then **`path_outcomes` in `sources.py`** — the cited outcome vector, 2 units, must land before CP2 Task 2/3 because that is what the rows will speak.

**P1 · CP2 revised (13 units).** Build the existing 11-task plan (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-27-cooking-paths-cp2.md`) with the owner's amendment folded in: rows say *what comes out*, the device sequence moves to the work plan. Start this **now**, not navigation — see the trigger list: NAV's own DoD line 1 says it cannot start until the owner answers §12 items 1–3 (the D5 reinterpretation, Back-at-root-leaves-the-app, and the loss of a single "close everything" gesture). CP2 is unblocked; NAV is not.

**P2 · Collagen index → `item_facts.py` → `rules.js` + `thresholds.py` (9 units).** In that order, strictly. `methodRules` decides the entire texture regime on "does `c.doneness` exist", while `app.js:1589` uses `c.tgt>=90` for the same purpose — an undeclared, uncited, duplicated model. If `rules.js` is written before the explicit collagen index, its `when` clauses re-derive regime from those two implicit models and the registry inherits the exact defect it exists to kill. **This phase is displaced by NAV the moment the owner answers §12** (see triggers).

**P3 · NAV Stage 1 + Stage A (7 units + 1 suite-repair unit).** Option B first (✕/Escape/backdrop → pop one), then `NAV` lands: the state object, `render` as the single DOM writer, `go`/`replace`/`commit`, `popstate`, `?nav=` on the existing document, the 5 funnels routed through it, and the `__legacy` descriptor with its **census test written RED**. This is the phase that delivers hardware Back and reload-restore of screen/wizard/catalog. The suite-repair unit: 8 spec files call `closePanel()` from `page.evaluate` (~28 sites) and `closePanel` becomes teardown-only — mechanical, bounded, one task.

**P4 · NAV Stage B + C (9 units).** Register the 43 class-A/B/C surfaces (mostly one line each), the three live launchers, `resolveItem`'s four key namespaces; then the class-D/E residue, the `openSeasonRecAI(backFn)` and `openEquipment(editId)` prerequisite refactors, delete `openTools` + `openPantry`'s dead body. Exit condition = the census test goes green. **After P4 the owner's #1 driver is fully delivered, on vanilla, at ~35 units — about three CP2-programmes in — with zero React.**

**P5 · Worker hardening (4 units — the ONE genuinely parallelizable stream).** `worker/index.js` lives in its own directory with its own vitest config, so this is the only work that does not contend for `app.js`. Fail-closed on corrupt KV, debit-before-forward, `AbortController` timeout, CORS off `*`, rate limit, close the `:streamGenerateContent` cap bypass. **Nothing user-owned may touch that Worker until this ships.**

**P6 · Keyspace & scope authority (6 units).** 66 `mk-*` keys, four incompatible scope namespaces, no migration registry (G-2), and — the killer — checkbox keys are the *translated label* (`'wpck:'+sc+':'+tk.label`, B13). This must precede any sync: two devices held in two languages generate two different key sets for the same tick, so syncing before this fix corrupts the user's own state across his own devices. Ship the schema + `mk-schema` migration registry + language-independent task identity.

**P7 · Accounts + encrypted export/import (6 units).** Billing provider hands back a signed token the Worker verifies; export/import is the zero-infra safety net and ships first as its own release.

**P8 · Sync on D1 (8 units).** Per-user blob, `updatedAt` LWW, background reconcile, localStorage stays source of truth, conflict UX. No CRDTs (single user, multiple devices — 04a-architecture §2b). **After P8 all three of the owner's drivers are delivered and React has still not been mentioned.**

**P9–P11 · The product roadmap (~75 units).** E4 → CP3 → CP4 → E5/E6; then P5a plan-pipeline extraction (`ORCH`) → the Phase-3a orchestrator solver; then P7 product surface (36 open F-band gaps: perf, a11y, tokens).

**PR · React — optional, last, and only under three conditions (30–45 units).** (1) `buildList` has been extracted by P5a — porting a render function that *writes user state while rendering* (B8) into a component reproduces the bug in a form that StrictMode and concurrent rendering make nondeterministic; (2) React output is bundled by esbuild into **one IIFE inlined by the existing `build.py`** — not a separate SPA deploy; (3) the **DOM contract is preserved** (same class names, same `data-*`, same `#panel`/`#appdlg` ids), which converts a 271-selector rewrite into approximately zero. Ported screen by screen, each one shippable.

**On the specific question about `rules.js`: yes, write it framework-agnostic NOW, and it changes the design in three concrete ways.** (a) It takes a **state snapshot as an argument** and returns typed codes — `rules.evaluate(snapshot) → [{code, params, cite, severity}]` — never reading `store` and never emitting prose; today's 13 decision sites all read state ambiently and emit Hebrew, and that ambient read is precisely what does not survive a component tree. (b) The **code→text mapping table lives in the render layer, not in `rules.js`** — vanilla maps code→HTML string today, React maps code→JSX later, and the registry never notices. (c) It follows the `equipment.js`/EQM pattern exactly: one narrow global, no ES modules, zero top-level calls (H2 ordering law), and a `build.py` F5 guard — which should be **extended for this module to also assert zero `document.` and zero `L(` occurrences in the file**, mechanically enforcing the purity that makes it survive. Note `equipment.js` already carries 0 `L()` calls, so the precedent is set and proven.

survives.asset: The Python data layer — data.py, sources.py (279 citations), equipment_map.py, descriptors, plus the new thresholds.py and item_facts.py
survives.survivesHow: React never touches it. It is compiled into the bundle by build.py and consumed as plain data. This is the single largest and most expensive asset in the repo and it is 100% framework-neutral.
survives.condition: Nothing. Keep safety constants out of any server (already the standing rule).

survives.asset: equipment.js / EQM, and every logic module extracted after it (rules.js, ORCH, the scheduler math, itemStages / effectiveSchedule / itemPaths)
survives.survivesHow: They are pure functions over data with one narrow global each. A React render layer calls them identically to how app.js calls them today. EQM already proves the pattern: 0 L() calls, 0 DOM.
survives.condition: Enforce purity mechanically NOW, at the second extraction: extend the F5 build guard so a module file must contain zero `document.` and zero `L(` occurrences. Without that guard the next module drifts back into DOM+prose and stops being portable.

survives.asset: The navigation descriptor registry (NAV) — the panel-id → JSON-params map, the restore classes A/B/C/D/E, the 57-surface inventory
survives.survivesHow: It IS a route table. React Router consumes `{id, p}` descriptors directly; the class-D/E honesty ceiling (11 surfaces that can only restore to their parent) is a product decision that carries over verbatim. This is why building it now rather than during a React port is the highest-leverage sequencing choice available.
survives.condition: Descriptors stay JSON-only and fail loudly at registration if they cannot round-trip through JSON.stringify — already normative in spec §5.2. Never let a closure back into a descriptor param.

survives.asset: The 816 Playwright tests — specifically the ~124 spec files that mock via window globals (gemFetch, __aiMock, __spoke, _wpCtx)
survives.survivesHow: They test the app through the real DOM with real clicks and localStorage seeds — that is framework-agnostic by construction. The window-global mocking survives because the logic modules keep exposing the same globals; React would own only render.
survives.condition: If React ever lands, preserve the DOM contract (class names, data-* attributes, element ids). This one rule is the difference between ~0 and ~271 broken locators.

survives.asset: The 23-language i18n corpus — ~1,300 chrome keys plus ~740 baked data values, and Guards A/B/C/D
survives.survivesHow: The dictionaries are keyed on the Hebrew source string harvested from static L(he,en) literals. If the call shape is preserved, a React port only needs the extractor to gain a JSX-capable parser — the keys and all 23 dictionaries are untouched.
survives.condition: NON-NEGOTIABLE: nobody 'modernizes' L('בשר','meat') into t('common.meat') during a React port. Re-keying is the single biggest avoidable loss in this whole programme — it would invalidate every dictionary and every Guard-A/D artifact at once. Write this into the React spec as a hard constraint before the first line of JSX.

survives.asset: build.py's single-file inline pipeline, the F5 module guards, and the Cloudflare Pages deploy
survives.survivesHow: esbuild emits one IIFE; build.py inlines it into __JS__ exactly as it inlines app.js and equipment.js today. The version stamp, the guards and the deploy are unchanged.
survives.condition: Do NOT adopt a separate SPA deploy or a dev server as the shipping path. Generalize build.py's hardcoded equipment.js block into a MODULES list at the second extraction (already the registered rule) so React's bundle is just another entry.

survives.asset: The Cloudflare Worker + D1 decision, and the existing matkonet-ai proxy seam
survives.survivesHow: Server-side and client-side are already separated by the GEM_HOST seam. Adding /sync to the same Worker on the same $5 bill needs no client framework at all.
survives.condition: Harden the Worker (P5) before any user-owned data goes near it — today it fails OPEN on corrupt KV and debits after the spend.

dies.asset: The HTML-string render layer — ~1,085 lines carrying HTML tags, 104 `innerHTML =` assignment sites, 395 addEventListener bindings
dies.whyLost: This is what React replaces. It is the genuine and only unavoidable rewrite, and it is roughly 15–20% of app.js's 11,564 lines. Being straight with the owner: this is the answer to 'what gets thrown away' — this, and nothing else that matters.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: Partly, and deliberately not entirely. Every screen ported keeps its CSS (app.css, 1,780 lines, untouched) and its DOM contract. The *markup* survives as JSX structure; only the string-concatenation plumbing dies. Port screen by screen so it is never a big bang.

dies.asset: The 271 `page.locator(...)` CSS selectors across 127 spec files
dies.whyLost: A render rewrite that changes class names or element structure invalidates them wholesale.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: YES — almost entirely, and this is a rule not a hope. Make DOM-contract preservation a hard acceptance criterion of any React port (same classes, same data-* attrs, same ids). Then the selectors keep passing and the suite becomes the regression harness *for* the port instead of a casualty of it. Skipping this rule turns a 3-unit suite cost into ~15.

dies.whyLost: Deliberately destroyed by NAV Stage A — closures cannot be serialized into a history entry or a URL, which is the root cause of every navigation defect.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: No, and we should not want to. It dies in P3 regardless of whether React ever happens. The replacement (descriptors) is strictly more capable.

dies.asset: The whole-body MutationObserver i18n hydration walk (app.js:11390) — 62% of non-Hebrew wall-clock in long tasks (F-8)
dies.whyLost: React's declarative render makes re-scanning the DOM for untranslated nodes unnecessary.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: It should die MUCH sooner than React, for 1–2 units, in P11 or opportunistically. Do not hold a real perf defect hostage to a framework decision — that would be using React to justify work that is cheaper without it.

dies.asset: `openTools` (29 lines) and `openPantry`'s unreachable panel body (34 lines)
dies.whyLost: Scheduled deletion in NAV Stage C per no-inert-shipment.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: No — `openTools`' *mechanism* (launcher records where it came from) is adopted as NAV.open() for all three live launchers; only its dead, un-i18n'd surface is deleted. The good part is preserved, the dead part is not.

triggers: **The owner answers navigation-spec §12 items 1–3** (the D5 `openTools` reinterpretation, whether Back at the root leaves the app, and whether losing a single 'close everything' gesture is acceptable) → NAV Stage 1+A starts at the next phase boundary and **displaces P2 (collagen/rules.js)** in the queue. Until then NAV cannot legally start — its own DoD line 1 requires those answers, and 'recorded in a document' does not count as raised.

**Any decision to store user-owned data on our infrastructure** (even a beta, even one tester) → P5 Worker hardening becomes blocking and must ship before a `/sync` route exists. Today the Worker fails OPEN on a corrupted KV record, debits after the spend, and runs CORS `*`.

**The second module extraction that carries user-facing strings** → generalize build.py's hardcoded equipment.js block into a MODULES list with per-module F5 guards, AND teach `scripts/i18n-extract.mjs` multi-file input, then regenerate `lang/_callsite-sig.json` and re-derive Guard D. `equipment.js` carried 0 L() calls so this cost has not been paid yet; the extractor and both its specs are still hardcoded to `app.js`.

**`buildList` is extracted from its render closure (P5a/ORCH ships)** → React becomes technically *evaluable*, and not one day before. Porting a render function that writes user state (B8) into a component is how a rewrite reproduces a bug in a worse form.

**A second developer joins, or the owner wants a component library / design system / hiring leverage** → the React ROI argument changes from 'fashion' to 'real'. Re-run this decision at that point; on today's inputs (solo owner, three named drivers none of which React addresses) it does not pay.

**`dist/index.html` passes ~10 MB, or cold LCP regresses past ~4s** → revisit the single-file PWA model itself. That is a bigger architectural question than React and should not be smuggled in as a side effect of one.

**Any request to see a live cook on two devices simultaneously** → that is not last-write-wins blob sync; it needs a Durable Object or WebSocket design. Escalate before designing — see the open question about what 'realtime' means.

risks.risk: Sync is built before the keyspace schema (P8 before P6). Checkbox keys are the *translated label* (`'wpck:'+sc+':'+tk.label`, gap B13) and there are four incompatible scope namespaces with no migration registry (G-2). Two of the owner's own devices held in two languages generate two different key sets for the same tick.
risks.mitigation: P6 is a hard gate on P8. Ship language-independent task identity, the scope authority, and an `mk-schema` migration registry first — and prove it with a two-language round-trip test before a single byte leaves the device.

risks.risk: React is attempted before P5a extracts `buildList`. Rendering the plan currently WRITES user state (`st.method`/`st.stage`/`st.ready`, then persists — gap B8). Under StrictMode double-render and concurrent rendering this becomes nondeterministic state corruption that the current architecture merely makes ugly.
risks.mitigation: Name P5a as a formal precondition of any React spec. No React task may be planned while `buildList` is still a nested closure that persists state during render.

risks.risk: The i18n corpus is re-keyed during a React port ('while we're here, let's use proper translation keys'). 23 languages × ~1,300 chrome keys + ~740 data values are all keyed on the Hebrew source string harvested by an acorn AST walk; Guard A/B/C/D and `lang/_callsite-sig.json` all depend on that scheme.
risks.mitigation: Write into the React spec, as a numbered non-negotiable: `L(he,en)` static two-literal calls survive verbatim; the extractor gains a JSX-capable parser (acorn-jsx, sourceType module), never a new key scheme. Add a build assertion that the extracted key count does not drop across the port.

risks.risk: 'Realtime' is implemented before it is defined. Device-convergence-in-seconds, live-cook-mirroring, and server-pushed content updates are three different architectures (LWW blobs / Durable Objects / cache invalidation) and only the first is costed in 04a-architecture.
risks.mitigation: Owner question, answered before P7 is planned. If the answer is live-cook mirroring, the D1-blob design in 04a §2b is insufficient and the phase must be re-specified — that is a spec change, so it goes through the owner, not around him.

risks.risk: Two streams edit `app.js` concurrently. NAV rewrites the 5 funnels, CP2 inserts into `openCut`, `rules.js` touches 13 decision sites — one 11,564-line file, and §11a already forbids concurrent suite runs.
risks.mitigation: Serialize everything that touches app.js. Exactly one stream is genuinely parallel — P5 Worker hardening, which lives in `worker/` with its own vitest config and shares no file. Run that one alongside; run nothing else alongside.

risks.risk: React is adopted partly to fix performance (cold LCP 2863, CLS 0.29, TBT 853, 7.8 MB dist). It does not fix any of it — the costs are parse time, unminified JS, 8 render-blocking Google Font families, and the i18n MutationObserver.
risks.mitigation: Do the ~3 units of actual perf work (minify, drop/self-host fonts, kill the observer) independently and measure. If the owner's React motivation was partly perf, that measurement removes it — or proves it was never the reason.

risks.risk: `__legacy` in NAV Stage A becomes permanent — the classic L2/DoD-5 inert-fallback failure, leaving an app where some panels restore and some silently do not.
risks.mitigation: Already designed: the census test (T15) sweeps all 58 launcher slots and asserts `__legacy` count === 0. It is written RED in Stage A and its going green is Stage B's exit condition. Do not let Stage B close without it.

risks.risk: CP2's per-recipe selected path (`mk-item-path`) gets re-litigated as a URL parameter when NAV's `?nav=` model lands, and is built twice.
risks.mitigation: Decide it now and write it down: the selected path is durable per-recipe DATA in the store, not view state in the URL. NAV registers `{id:'cut', p:{key}}` and nothing more. Two mechanisms for one value is how the 13 scattered decision sites happened.

effort:
**Unit = one task like a CP2 task** (the CP2 plan is 11 such tasks / ~150 code blocks / 4,330 plan lines, RED→GREEN + i18n in 6 active languages + full-suite gate). So **1 CP2-programme = 11 units.**

| Phase | Content | Units |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Wave 0 (wrap-as-stage, svOrderDesc, validCombo) + `path_outcomes` in sources.py | **6** |
| P1 | CP2 revised (rows speak outcome; device order in the work plan) | **13** |
| P2 | Collagen index → item_facts.py → rules.js + thresholds.py | **9** |
| P3 | NAV Stage 1 + Stage A (+1 suite repair: 8 files, ~28 `closePanel()` call sites) | **8** |
| P4 | NAV Stage B + C (register 43 surfaces, class-D/E residue, prereq refactors, deletions) | **9** |
| P5 | Worker hardening — **the only genuinely parallel stream** (own directory, own vitest) | **4** |
| P6 | Keyspace schema, scope authority, `mk-schema` migration registry, B13 task identity | **6** |
| P7 | Accounts (signed billing token) + encrypted export/import | **6** |
| P8 | D1 sync: per-user blob, LWW, background reconcile, conflict UX | **8** |
| **Subtotal — all three owner drivers delivered** | | **~69 (≈6.3 CP2-programmes)** |
| P9 | E4 → CP3 → CP4 → E5/E6 | ~30 |
| P10 | P5a plan-pipeline extraction (ORCH) → Phase-3a orchestrator solver | ~25 |
| P11 | P7 product surface — 36 open F-band gaps (perf, a11y, tokens) | ~20 |
| **PR** | **React — optional, last:** toolchain 4 · ~60 surfaces ported at ~4/unit ≈ 20–25 · suite 3 (with DOM contract) or 15 (without) | **30–45** |

**Critical path: P0 → P1 → P3 → P4 → P5 → P6 → P7 → P8.** (P2 is the only phase that can be displaced — by NAV, the moment the owner answers §12.)

**THE ONE DECISION THAT COSTS THE MOST IF MADE WRONG: whether the navigation descriptor model is built NOW on vanilla, or deferred into the React migration.** Defer it and you pay four times — navigation stays broken for the entire months-long duration of the port; the port must invent the same 57-surface descriptor model anyway, but without the 816-test safety net because the selectors break in the same commits; the restore-class analysis (43 restorable, 11 parent-only, 3 never — already done and paid for in the spec) gets redone from scratch; and the owner's daily pain is the last thing fixed instead of the first. Build it now and it ships in ~16 units, the owner feels it immediately, and the artifact **becomes React Router's route table for free**. Everything else in this plan is reorderable at some cost; this one is a 4× multiplier.

**The two numbers the owner should hold on to.** Navigation — his #1 stated pain — is **fully delivered at ~35 units, about three CP2-programmes in, with zero React**. React costs **30–45 units for zero user-visible feature** — three to four CP2-programmes of pure re-plumbing. That ratio is the whole answer: the drivers are cheap and the framework is expensive, and they are not the same purchase.
openQuestions: **Is React a goal or a means?** If the goal is 'working navigation, multi-device sync, and a UI I can keep changing', the plan above delivers all three and React is optional forever. If React is wanted for its own sake — component ecosystem, a design system, hiring, familiarity, wanting to use a library — say so plainly. That changes the answer from 'probably never' to 'scheduled, last, and here is what it costs'. It is a legitimate reason; it is just not one of the three drivers named, and pricing it honestly requires knowing it exists.

**What exactly does 'עדכניות realtime' mean?** Three different products: (a) my phone and my PC converge within seconds of each other — LWW blobs on D1, as costed; (b) a cook running on my phone is visible live on my PC while it runs — needs Durable Objects or WebSockets, a different and larger design; (c) catalog/content updates pushed from the server without a reinstall — a cache-invalidation problem, cheapest of the three. P7/P8 cannot be planned until this is answered.

**The three blocking navigation answers (spec §12.1–3),** which its own DoD line 1 requires before any code: (1) revive `openTools` as specified in D5-A, or adopt its mechanism and delete its surface — the recommendation, which is outcome-closer to D5-B and therefore a spec reinterpretation that must be raised in conversation; (2) does Back at the root leave the app (platform convention, but a mis-tap closes an installed PWA mid-cook); (3) is losing 'close everything' as a single gesture acceptable — from three deep it becomes three presses.

**Are you willing to pick an identity/payment provider now?** Accounts gate sync, and sync is driver #3. Stripe/Paddle/Lemon Squeezy handing back a signed token the Worker verifies keeps all PII and payment data off our infrastructure — but it is a commitment, and P7 cannot be planned around a provider that has not been chosen.

**Does CP2 or navigation go first if the §12 answers arrive tomorrow?** My recommendation is CP2 first — it is planned to task level and its approval is fresh — but navigation is what you feel every day (your own D4 discussion said exactly that), and the re-anchoring cost of doing NAV first is under a unit because the CP2 plan already re-derives its anchors by symbol. If daily pain outranks momentum, say so and I will reorder P1 and P3. This is genuinely your call, not ours.

**Do you want auto-dark (F-23)?** It was WAIVED on mechanism grounds — the app themes at runtime via JS, so `prefers-color-scheme` was removed as dead code — but the underlying UX concern (bright cream default at 02:00, mid-cook) was never solved by anything else. It is cheap in P11 if you want it and should not be silently inherited as 'closed'.

**Is the single-file PWA model itself still the commitment?** `dist/index.html` is 7.8 MB. Everything above assumes it holds and that React (if ever) bundles into the same single inlined script. If you would accept a normal multi-file bundle with code splitting, several perf gaps get much cheaper — but it is a bigger architectural change than React and deserves its own decision, not a side effect of one.
